newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Repo market first test of EMU efficiency - ISMA.
newsitem.headline: Repo market first test of EMU efficiency - ISMA.

text.p: Any problems relating to the introduction of the single European currency in 1999 are likely to be felt first by the repo market, the International Securities Market Association (ISMA) said on Thursday.

With turnover of $25 trillion in Europe in 1996, the repo market is settlement-intensive, and any problems with the euro are likely to show up there first, a report commissioned by ISMA and released at its annual general meeting in Singapore said.

"The chances of total chaos on January 4, 1999 are low: perhaps one percent," the report, written by ISMA Centre Director Professor Brian Scott-Quinn and Julian Walmsley, visiting research fellow at the Centre, said.

"The chances of relatively high incidence of settlement failures are much higher: perhaps 20 percent. The chances of at least one major firm having a software problem which may ripple over to other firms are higher still," it said.

The report added that systems complexities were in danger of being seriously underestimated, and called on governments to make practical decisions regarding European economic and monetary union (EMU) as soon as possible.

The repo, or repurchase, market works by allowing central banks and other market participants to borrow securities for short periods to fund positions. The market is crucial for the operation of monetary policy, and is widely used to hedge positions, making it a vital tool in risk management.
The report said governments needed to take decisions urgently on practical matters relating to EMU to avoid making the transition more difficult, expensive and risky.
The key problems were weak linkages between domestic depositories and the implicit risk of "ripple" settlement failure across the euro area arising from failure of these linkages.
National legal systems were not well-adapted to cross-border activity and different tax treatments remained across Europe regarding withholding tax and turnover tax, the report said.

There were also question marks over the relationship between the European Central Bank and national central banks. National central banks were determined to prevent any activity being carried out by the ECB, unless absolutely necessary, the report said.
But it remained unclear who would coordinate euro liquidity in a crisis, the report said.

Outstanding practical issues included value date conventions, which would become vital from January 1, 1998 because some market participants trade out to one year. Also, time is needed to develop changes in software to cope with new

"The repo market is closely linked to government bond trading activity, the futures market for government bonds, the market for interest rate swaps and bond options, and last but not least other short-term money markets," the report said.
"Hence it is one of the key operating components of a modern financial system."
